<reason>Both sides were sharp, but CON (A) won more of the decisive exchanges. A's central fork — the bare notice is either impotent (an always-on signal that discriminates nothing and enables no complaint) or a Trojan horse for the criteria disclosure B expressly disavowed — was never dismantled. A turned B's two best analogies: nutrition labels work by listing ingredients (the very thing B1.6 refused), and credit adverse-action notices fire on specific decisions, name reasons, and attach to a correctable file — features the dating banner lacks; B dropped both. A answered both pressure questions directly and consistently, naming targeted disclosures (boost labels, data access) that escape the fork rather than conceding it, making B's "the debate ended at A4.3" spin an overclaim (and "pressed across three rounds" a misdescription). Critically, A's mechanism that machine-blame is unfalsifiable and drives boost purchases — worsening B's own core harm — went unanswered in B's last two speeches. B's door-not-house and admission theories were attractive but dented by A's point that regulators subpoena and no app claims an organic pool. A's closing surgically exposed the gap between the rich fact B wants users to have and the thin sentence the motion mandates. A's two clipped turns are a real execution cost, keeping the margin modest.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 1 turning the nutrition-facts analogy: labels inform by listing ingredients, so the honest dating-app equivalent is criteria disclosure — which B had explicitly disavowed — leaving B's best analogy defending a right B refused to defend; B never rehabilitated it.</best_rebuttal>
